patients.summary: Retired pharmaceutical sales rep with CAD, old MI with a stent, ischemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension and hyperlipidemia who joins in 2020, develops essential tremor and stable angina, and is last seen in October 2024. Afterward the chart receives late outside records of a 2025 cardiology visit, a 2026 VF arrest with post-hypoxic myoclonus and post-MI pericarditis, and a 2026 Weber syndrome stroke.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

Raymond is a 64 year old man joining us from a primary care office out of town. He retired this spring after a long career selling pharmaceuticals, mostly to cardiology and internal medicine offices, so he knows his drugs better than most.

Cardiac history (his account; records requested): remote myocardial infarction treated with cardiac catheterization and a drug-eluting stent. He was told afterward that the heart muscle was weakened (ischemic cardiomyopathy). He does not remember the ejection fraction number. Sees an outside cardiology group about once a year and wants to keep them. No chest pain. Walks the neighborhood most days, no exertional symptoms with that. No orthopnea, no leg swelling, no palpitations, no fainting.

Also hypertension and high cholesterol for many years.

MEDS (bottles reviewed): aspirin 81 mg daily; metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Takes them every day, uses a pill box.
ALLERGIES: none to medications.
SURGICAL: cardiac cath with PCI/DES as above. Nothing else.
FAMILY: father had an MI at 59. Mother had high blood pressure and high cholesterol. Brother has a tremor that a neurologist called essential tremor. Paternal uncle had a stroke at 64.
SOCIAL: married, lives with his wife. Smoked about 30 pack-years and quit in 2015. Wine 2 to 3 glasses a week. No other substances.
PREVENTION per his recollection: colonoscopy a couple of years ago, told it was clean. Thinks he had a tetanus shot in 2017. Has never had a lung CT.

ROS: otherwise negative in detail.

EXAM: vitals as charted. Well appearing, pleasant. HEENT normal. Neck supple, no JVD, no carotid bruit. Heart regular rate and rhythm, no murmur or gallop. Lungs clear throughout. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities warm, no edema, distal pulses 2+. Neuro grossly nonfocal, no tremor noted.

ASSESSMENT/PLAN
1. CAD with old MI, stent in place; ischemic cardiomyopathy, clinically compensated. Continue aspirin, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril, atorvastatin. Records from cardiology requested so we have his echo history here.
2. Hypertension: office reading above goal today; he says home readings run in the 120s-130s. Recheck with his home cuff log at the next visit, no change now.
3. Hyperlipidemia: lipid panel today on atorvastatin 40.
4. Lung cancer screening: eligible (30 pack-years, quit within 15 years). Discussed annual low-dose CT; he wants it. Ordered.
5. Health maintenance: CMP, CBC, lipids, A1c, one-time hepatitis C and HIV screening, all accepted. Flu shot next month once the nurse clinic opens. Colonoscopy and Tdap to be confirmed from old records.

Follow up in about 4 months, sooner as needed.

The lung CT order went to scheduling and they should call you this week.

LOW-DOSE CT CHEST, LUNG CANCER SCREENING (baseline)
Indication: 64 year old former smoker, 30 pack-years, quit 2015.
Technique: low-dose helical CT of the chest without contrast.
Findings: Lungs clear without nodule, mass or consolidation. Airways patent. No pleural effusion. Heart normal in size; coronary artery calcification and a coronary stent. No pericardial effusion. No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable. Bones without suspicious lesion.

documents.title: Office Visit - Tremor
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: shaky hands.

HPI: Since late summer, roughly four months, both hands shake when he holds something: coffee cup, a fork, signing checks. His wife noticed first. Not there when his hands rest in his lap. It is a little better after a glass of wine, which he says with some embarrassment. No new drugs; meds are the same four for years. No caffeine change, no palpitations, no weight loss, no heat intolerance. No stiffness, no slowness, no falls, no change in his walking. His brother has a tremor diagnosed as essential tremor.

Exam: BP and pulse as charted. Thyroid not enlarged. Fine tremor of both hands with arms held out and on finger-nose, no tremor at rest. No cogwheeling, normal arm swing, normal fast finger taps. Gait normal. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P: Bilateral action/postural tremor, family history in a brother, alcohol-responsive. Most consistent with essential tremor; no parkinsonian features. Thyroid function and BMP today. Referred to neurology to confirm.

RTC after neurology.

documents.title: Thyroid results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thyroid tests are normal, as are calcium and the rest of the chemistries, so the tremor isn't coming from the thyroid. Neurology referral is in; their office will call you.

documents.title: Neurology Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 01/30/2023
Referred by primary care for bilateral hand tremor.

Dear colleague,

I saw Mr. Alden, 66, who describes about six months of shaking in both hands. It is worst when he holds a coffee cup or writes, and he has noticed it settles after alcohol. He has no tremor when his hands are at rest.

History includes hypertension on lisinopril, hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin, coronary artery disease with prior MI and stent, and ischemic cardiomyopathy. Medications: aspirin 81 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. NKDA. Brother with essential tremor; father MI at 59; mother hypertension and hyperlipidemia; paternal uncle stroke at 64. Former smoker (30 pack-years, quit 2015), 2-3 glasses of wine weekly, retired pharmaceutical sales.

Examination: Postural tremor of both upper extremities. No rigidity. No bradykinesia on repetitive tasks. Finger-nose and heel-shin without dysmetria; no other cerebellar signs. Cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation and gait otherwise normal.

Data: routine labs from your office, including thyroid function, are normal.

Impression: Essential tremor. No features of parkinsonism or cerebellar disease.

Plan: return to neurology clinic in follow-up.

Neurology

documents.title: Follow-up - Angina
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up after cardiology (2/5). We still have no letter, so this is from his account.

He says cardiology told him it is stable angina from his coronary disease and that they will manage it with medicine for now. ECG there showed nothing acute and his cholesterol panel was fine. He came in having read about a newly approved angina drug and asked for it instead of the usual approach; the cardiologist explained it has little long-term data and is not a first choice, and gave him nitroglycerin tablets to carry. He has used one tablet once, on a cold morning, with relief in a couple of minutes. Episodes with brisk walking or hills, a few a week, brief. None at rest.

Meds: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, SL NTG prn (outside Rx).

Exam: vitals as charted. Regular, soft systolic murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P:
1. Stable angina, CAD. Added to problem list. Reviewed NTG use: sit down, one tablet, repeat every 5 minutes up to 3, call 911 if not better after the first. Keep tablets in the original bottle. No PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates; he takes none.
2. Ischemic cardiomyopathy, HTN: unchanged.
3. Request cardiology visit note again.

RTC at the physical, sooner prn.

OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY - FOLLOW-UP
Date of visit: 08/02/2024

Mr. Alden is a 68 year old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CAD with prior MI, and ischemic cardiomyopathy whom I first saw in January 2023 for hand tremor. He reports that over about two years the tremor in both hands has gradually worsened. It is worse with action, such as drinking from a cup or writing, and less obvious at rest. It does not wake him. No stiffness, slowness, imbalance or other neurologic symptoms.

Medications: aspirin 81 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, nitroglycerin SL as needed. NKDA. Social and family history unchanged from my prior note.

Exam: bilateral postural hand tremor. No rigidity, no bradykinesia. Handwriting sample: large, wavy letters with a steady oscillation; no decrement in letter size across the line. Gait normal, pull test negative.

Impression: Essential tremor, slowly progressive. Exam continues to show no parkinsonian features.

Plan: follow-up in neurology clinic as needed.

Neurology

Pericardium: no effusion.
reports.conclusion: Calcified aortic valve, valve area 1.5 cm2. Normal left ventricular systolic function, LVEF 55%.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received by fax after request)
Admitted: 01/28/2026  Discharged: 02/10/2026

Principal diagnosis: Out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest due to acute myocardial infarction.
Secondary diagnoses: post-hypoxic myoclonic status epilepticus, resolved; post-infarction pericarditis with recurrent pericardial effusion; ischemic cardiomyopathy; coronary artery disease with prior stent; hypertension; hyperlipidemia; essential tremor.

History: 69 year old man who collapsed without warning at home while walking to the kitchen. His wife called 911 and began chest compressions. EMS found ventricular fibrillation; three shocks were delivered by AED with return of spontaneous circulation. On arrival he was comatose, GCS 6, and was intubated.

ICU course: Admission vitals T 37.2 C, BP 110/70, HR 88, RR 16 on the ventilator. He had continuous, generalized, symmetric myoclonic jerking of the face, trunk and limbs, consistent with post-hypoxic myoclonic status epilepticus. EEG showed no epileptiform discharges. Treated with sedation and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. Admission chemistries: Na 140, K 4.2, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, Cr 1.1, glucose 98, Ca 9.2, Mg 2.0, phos 3.5; CBC normal; ABG pH 7.40 / PaCO2 40 / PaO2 95. Cardiology attributed the arrest to acute myocardial infarction. Myoclonus subsided over the following days; extubated 01/31 and awake, following commands.

Hospital day 4 (02/01): new sharp left chest pain, worse with deep breaths and lying flat; rub on exam; see cardiology consult. Small effusion on echo, no tamponade. Colchicine started. Effusion trace on 02/04, then small again on 02/09 without hemodynamic effect; managed conservatively, no drainage.

Levetiracetam stopped 02/08 with no recurrence of myoclonus. Worked with PT/OT, ambulating independently at discharge.

Discharge medications:
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- atorvastatin 40 mg nightly
- colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months (new)
- nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL prn
Allergies: NKDA.

Disposition: home with wife. Follow-up: cardiology in 2 weeks with repeat echocardiogram; primary care within 1 to 2 weeks.

Hospitalist service

documents.title: Inpatient Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
INPATIENT CARDIOLOGY CONSULT - 02/01/2026 (hospital day 4)
Reason: new chest pain.

69 year old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy admitted four days ago with acute MI complicated by VF arrest, now extubated. This morning he developed a sharp left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration and when he lies back. He says it does not feel like the pain he had four days ago.

Meds in hospital: aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin, lisinopril; levetiracetam.

BP 130/85, HR 88, RR 18.
Exam: pericardial friction rub. Lungs clear.
Labs: WBC 11.0, Hgb 14.2, platelets 250, creatinine 1.0.
ECG: sinus rhythm, no new changes compared with prior.
Echo: small circumferential effusion, no tamponade; LVEF 45%.

Impression: early post-infarction pericarditis with small pericardial effusion.
Recommendations: colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months; continue aspirin; avoid other NSAIDs; serial limited echoes. No drainage indicated.

Cardiology

documents.title: Call from wife
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt's wife called. Ray collapsed at home last evening, his heart stopped, she did CPR until the ambulance came and they shocked him three times. He is in the ICU at the regional hospital on a breathing machine and has been having jerking movements. She wanted us to know. Offered support; she has family with her. PCP informed.

documents.title: Call from wife
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called her back. Gave her our direct line for anything she needs, including help talking with the ICU team. Asked to be kept posted.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Wife answered; Ray came home yesterday. He's walking around the house, tired, chest pain much better. They have the discharge papers but no summary has come to us. She says there is a new pill for the heart lining. Cardiology appointment in two weeks. Offered a transitional care visit this week or next; she said she'd talk with him and call back. No callback by end of week. Hospital records requested.

documents.title: Discharge summary received
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Discharge summary and cardiology consult received and reviewed. VF arrest from acute MI, post-hypoxic myoclonus resolved, post-MI pericarditis with recurrent small effusion on colchicine. Still no office visit since discharge; asked front desk to reach out again.

REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT - PHYSICIAN NOTE (copy received by fax)
Date of visit: 07/21/2026

CC: drooping left eyelid and right-sided weakness.

HPI: 70 year old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy, essential tremor, and a cardiac arrest in January 2026, brought in with a left eyelid droop and his left eye turned out and down, which began together with weakness of his right arm and leg. No headache, no dizziness, no loss of consciousness.

Meds per wife: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40. NKDA.

Vitals: BP 165/95, HR 78, RR 16.
Neuro: left ptosis; left pupil dilated and unreactive to light; left eye deviated down and laterally. Right upper and lower extremities 3/5 with normal tone and reflexes. Sensation intact.

CT head without contrast: no hemorrhage, no mass effect.

Impression: left oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis, Weber syndrome, consistent with left midbrain infarction.
Disposition: stroke team evaluated in the ED; admitted to the stroke service.

Emergency Medicine
